title: Two Pauses of Breath
essence: This is the closing gap at the top of the inhale and the bottom of the exhale — the two brief, naturally-occurring stillnesses that every breath already contains, whether or not anyone notices them. The technique is not a breathing exercise in the sense of controlling the breath; it's a noticing exercise aimed at the space breath leaves behind. The invitation is to notice whether attention placed in an already-still point feels any different from attention placed on movement.
script:
Find a position where your spine can be upright without effort — seated is fine, standing is fine. Let your eyes close, or soften your gaze toward the floor a few feet ahead.

For a few breaths, just breathe normally. Don't change anything yet. Notice the air moving in, and the air moving out.

Now bring your attention to the very top of the inhale — that brief moment after the in-breath finishes and before the out-breath begins. There's a small pause there. Most of the time we breathe right through it without noticing. This time, when you reach it, let your attention rest there. Don't hold your breath on purpose — just notice the pause that's already happening.

Breathe out. And now find the other pause — the one at the bottom of the exhale, right before the next inhale starts. Rest your attention there too, for as long as it naturally lasts.

Keep going like this: breathe normally, and each time you arrive at one of the two pauses, let your attention settle into it rather than rushing past it toward the next breath.

If your mind wanders to something else entirely, that's fine — just come back to the next pause, whichever one arrives first.

In the last few breaths, stop trying to find the pauses precisely, and just let your attention rest in the general area of "in between." Notice whatever quality that space has — stillness, spaciousness, or simply the absence of the breath's motion.

When you're ready, let your breathing return to whatever rhythm it wants, and open your eyes.
source:
Verse: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra, verse 24 (with verse 25 as a direct continuation/clarification of the same practice — the two are often treated as a single dhāraṇā).

Translation cited: Christopher Wallis ("Hareesh"), *A Translation of the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra* (complete but lacking commentary), self-published 2017, revised 2018, distributed via hareesh.org. Wallis is a Sanskrit scholar (PhD, Oxford) and author of *Tantra Illuminated*; this is his direct verse-by-verse translation from the Sanskrit, not a secondhand paraphrase.

Guided text is a modern adaptation, not a literal translation.

title: Resting in the Pause
essence: This technique takes the same pause explored in Technique 01 and asks the practitioner to stay in it slightly longer — not by force, but by choice. Where Technique 01 is about *noticing* an already-brief gap, this one is about *staying with* it just enough to feel its texture.
script:
Sit comfortably, spine tall but not rigid. Rest your hands in your lap. Close your eyes if that's comfortable.

Breathe normally, without counting or changing the breath. Each time the breath reaches one of its natural pauses — after the in-breath or after the out-breath — let your attention stay in that stillness a little longer, without holding the breath to make the pause last. Let each pause be a place to rest, not a place to push through.

After a while, notice if anything in your body has started to settle — the shoulders, the jaw, the space between your eyebrows. You're not trying to make this happen; you're only noticing if it does.

Toward the end, breathe however feels natural, and see if the same settled quality you found in the pauses is still available, even without deliberately creating it.

Open your eyes when you're ready.
source:
Verse: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra, verse 27.

Translation cited: Christopher Wallis ("Hareesh"), *A Translation of the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra* (2017, rev. 2018, hareesh.org).

Guided text is a modern adaptation, not a literal translation.

title: Silence After the Hum
essence: The sound itself is only half the practice; the other half is what's left when the sound stops. This technique uses a hum as a way of manufacturing a clean, noticeable silence to land in — the silence is the actual destination, and the hum is just the vehicle that gets you there and then gets out of the way.
script:
Sit somewhere you won't feel self-conscious making a low sound out loud.

Let a soft, low hum sound naturally, without changing the breath — like the sound "mmm" or "ohm," whichever feels more natural in your throat. Let the hum fade out gently on its own rather than stopping it abruptly.

When the hum ends, stay in the silence that's left behind — notice it specifically, the way you'd notice a room after a loud noise stops.

Then repeat: let a hum sound naturally, without changing the breath, then pause to notice the silence after it fades.

Let the hum get quieter each time if that feels right — even a whispered or silent, internal version of the hum later on, if you want to try that.

Toward the end, skip the hum altogether and just sit in silence — see if you can find that same quality of "just after a sound has ended," even without a sound to end.

Sit quietly before opening your eyes.
source:
Verse: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra, verse 39 (with verse 40 as a closely related generalization of the same principle to any sound).

Translation cited: Christopher Wallis ("Hareesh"), *A Translation of the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra* (2017, rev. 2018, hareesh.org).

Guided text is a modern adaptation, not a literal translation.

title: The Fading Tone
essence: Most listening is aimed at the loudest, most obvious part of a sound. This technique redirects listening toward the opposite end: the long, quiet decay most people stop attending to as soon as a sound stops being "interesting." Following a tone all the way to silence asks for a kind of sustained, effortless attention that doesn't need a strong stimulus to stay engaged.
script:
Sit where you can hear clearly, ideally somewhere quiet. Have your sound source ready — strike it, pluck it, or play the recording once you're settled.

Close your eyes. Produce the tone (or start the recording), and let your attention land fully on the sound the moment it begins.

Follow the tone continuously as it changes — don't just note "there's a sound" and drift off. Track how it shifts: from full and bright, to softer, to thinner, all the way down to the quietest edge where you're not sure anymore whether you're still hearing it or just remembering it.

When the tone fades below hearing, stay with that edge for a moment — the point where sound and silence are hard to tell apart.

Produce the tone again (or replay it), and repeat the same close tracking, start to finish.

Each time, try to catch the tone a little earlier in its decay and follow it a little further than before.

After the tone has fully faded for the last time, stay seated in the resulting quiet before opening your eyes — see if the surrounding silence sounds any different than it did before you started.
source:
Verse: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra, verse 41.

Translation cited: Christopher Wallis ("Hareesh"), *A Translation of the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra* (2017, rev. 2018, hareesh.org): the verse describes one "whose heart-mind is completely focused on the prolonged sounds of a musical instrument such as a *tantrī* [a stringed instrument like a vīṇā], through the duration of the phases [of their resonance], at the limit [of the perceptible sound]."

Guided text is a modern adaptation, not a literal translation.

title: Sky Gazing
essence: An unbroken, soft gaze on something with no edges, no texture, and nothing to track gives the visual system nothing to chase. The technique isn't about the sky being special; it's about the sky being one of the few genuinely featureless things most people have easy daily access to.
script:
Find a spot where you can see a wide stretch of sky without straining your neck — sitting or standing, whichever lets you stay still and comfortable.

Let your gaze settle on the sky, somewhere open and empty rather than on a cloud, a bird, or a plane. Don't stare hard — let your eyes rest there the way they would rest on something plain and unremarkable.

Keep your body still. Let your shoulders drop, your jaw unclench. You're not trying to "see" anything — there's nothing to find. You're just letting your eyes stay in one open space.

If your eyes drift to something with an edge — a rooftop, a tree line, a cloud — gently bring them back to the emptiest part of the sky you can find.

Stay like this for a while. Notice, without forcing it, whether your visual field starts to feel wider than usual — and whether your peripheral vision seems to open up, almost like you're seeing "around" the point you're looking at, not just "at" it.

If your eyes get tired, blink normally — this isn't a stare-without-blinking exercise, just an unhurried, resting gaze.

When you're ready, let your gaze come back down to eye level, take a breath, and carry on with your day.
source:
Verse: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra, verse 84.

Translation cited: Christopher Wallis ("Hareesh"), *A Translation of the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra* (2017, rev. 2018, hareesh.org).

Guided text is a modern adaptation, not a literal translation.

title: Dappled Light
essence: Where Technique 05 (sky gazing) lets the eyes rest on total visual blankness, this technique uses the opposite: a busy, shifting, but non-demanding pattern of light and shadow. There's nothing to identify or track — no object, no shape holding still long enough to name — just movement and contrast. The attention has something to rest *on* without having anything to *solve*.
script:
Find or create a patch of broken, moving light — sunlight coming through leaves onto the ground, light through a curtain, or the flicker a candle throws on a wall nearby. Sit where you can watch it without straining.

Let your gaze settle on the pattern. Don't try to follow any single spot of light — let your attention spread across the whole moving texture, the way you'd watch a fire without picking out one particular flame.

Notice the movement without naming it. You don't need to describe what's happening — just let the shifting light and shadow hold your attention loosely, the way background music holds attention without demanding it.

If you catch yourself narrating ("that leaf moved," "that's a bright spot"), that's fine — just let the narration fade and return to watching without commentary.

Stay with this for a while. If your mind drifts entirely away from the light and into unrelated thoughts, gently bring your eyes and attention back to the pattern whenever you notice.

Toward the end, notice whether your overall state feels any different — looser, quieter, more spread out — without needing it to.

When you're ready, look away and blink a few times before continuing your day.
source:
Verse: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra, verse 76.

Translation cited: Christopher Wallis ("Hareesh"), *A Translation of the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra* (2017, rev. 2018, hareesh.org).

Guided text is a modern adaptation, not a literal translation.

title: The Gentle Swing
essence: Slow, rhythmic, self-paced movement — the kind a swing or a rocking chair provides — offers an experience distinct from stillness-based practices. This technique asks the practitioner to notice that experience directly, rather than just enjoying it passively, which is the difference between rocking as a pleasant habit and rocking as a deliberate attention practice.
script:
Settle into a rocking chair, swing, or hammock — or if none is available, stand with your feet hip-width apart, ready to sway gently from side to side.

Begin a slow, easy rocking motion — nothing fast or effortful, just a comfortable back-and-forth or side-to-side rhythm you could sustain without thinking about it.

Close your eyes if that feels stable, or keep a soft, unfocused gaze if you'd rather.

At first, just let the rocking happen and notice the physical sensation of it — the shift of weight, the small motion in your stomach or chest, the rhythm itself.

Now let your attention rest specifically on the *turning points* — the exact moment at each end of the rock where the direction changes, where you're neither quite going one way nor the other yet. There's a brief, almost weightless pause there, similar to the pause at the top or bottom of a breath.

Continue rocking gently, noticing each turning point as it arrives.

Let the rocking slow naturally, on its own, without forcing it to stop. As it slows, notice whether your internal state has shifted at all, and if so, how.

When the rocking has mostly stopped, sit for a few still breaths before opening your eyes.
source:
Verse: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra, verse 83.

Translation cited: Christopher Wallis ("Hareesh"), *A Translation of the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra* (2017, rev. 2018, hareesh.org).

Guided text is a modern adaptation, not a literal translation.

title: Savoring Fully
essence: This is one of the more directly usable verses in the text: it doesn't ask the practitioner to imagine anything or adopt a special posture, only to pay full, undistracted attention to a pleasure that is already happening — the taste of food — instead of letting it pass by unnoticed the way eating usually does when it's rushed or paired with a screen.
script:
Have your chosen food or drink in front of you. Put away your phone and anything else that would normally have your attention while eating.

Before taking a bite or sip, pause and look at what you're about to taste — really look at it, noticing color, texture, anything you'd normally skip past.

Take a small first bite or sip. Don't swallow right away — let it sit in your mouth for a moment and notice the first wave of flavor as fully as you can.

Swallow, and notice what remains afterward — the aftertaste, the warmth or coolness, whatever lingers.

Take a second bite or sip, slower this time than you normally would. Notice if the flavor is the same as the first taste, or if it's shifted slightly now that you're paying closer attention.

Continue eating or drinking at this slower pace, treating each bite or sip as the only thing happening right now — no multitasking, no rushing to the next one.

Notice, without needing to name it precisely, whether there's a felt sense of satisfaction or fullness that builds as you continue — not just in your stomach, but as a general quality of the experience.

When you're finished, sit for a breath or two before moving on, rather than immediately jumping to the next task.
source:
Verse: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra, verse 72.

Translation cited: Christopher Wallis ("Hareesh"), *A Translation of the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra* (2017, rev. 2018, hareesh.org).

Guided text is a modern adaptation, not a literal translation.

title: The Gap Between Two
essence: Most attention lives inside thoughts and states, moving from one to the next without noticing the seam between them. This technique treats that seam — the interval where one thing has ended and the next hasn't started — as a legitimate place to rest attention, rather than as a gap to be filled as quickly as possible.
script:
Sit comfortably and let your eyes close. Don't try to think about anything in particular — just let your mind do what it normally does.

At first, simply notice thoughts arising and passing, the way you'd notice cars going by. Don't follow any of them, don't push any away — just notice that they come and go.

Now shift the aim slightly: instead of watching the thoughts themselves, try to catch the moment between one thought ending and the next one starting. It will be brief — but there's a small window there where nothing in particular is happening.

When you catch that window, however briefly, let your attention rest there rather than immediately following whatever thought comes next.

This is subtle and you'll miss it often — that's completely normal. Each time you notice a thought has already started pulling your attention along, that noticing itself is useful; just look for the next gap.

From here, keep gently aiming for that in-between space, without frustration if it's hard to find. It's less something you do and more something you notice when your usual habit of chasing the next thought briefly loosens.

Toward the end, drop the effort to find the gap deliberately, and just sit quietly, letting thoughts come and go however they will.

Open your eyes slowly when you're ready.
source:
Verse: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra, verse 61 (with verse 62 as a direct continuation of the same instruction).

Translation cited: Christopher Wallis ("Hareesh"), *A Translation of the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra* (2017, rev. 2018, hareesh.org).

Guided text is a modern adaptation, not a literal translation.

title: Threshold of Sleep
essence: This technique doesn't ask the practitioner to create anything; it asks them to notice something that already happens most nights and usually gets missed because it's so brief and because the natural next step is unconsciousness. The hypnagogic state — awake enough to notice, relaxed enough that ordinary thinking has mostly stopped — is treated here as worth a moment of deliberate attention rather than being slept straight through.
duration: 3–5 minutes (at bedtime, self-paced — may end early if sleep arrives)
script:
This one is done lying in bed, lights off, at the point where you're genuinely getting sleepy — not as an alerting exercise, but as something to notice on the way down.

Let your body settle into the bed fully. Don't fight the drowsiness or try to stay sharply alert — that would defeat the point.

As the sounds around you start to fade into the background, and the pull to think in full sentences starts to loosen, notice that shift is happening. You don't need to hold onto it or analyze it — just a light, passing acknowledgment: "this is that in-between place."

If a clear thought or a mental image show up, don't chase it and don't push it away — let it pass through the same way you'd let it pass in a light doze.

There's no goal here beyond noticing you're in that particular state while you're in it, for as long as it naturally lasts before sleep takes over. If you fall asleep before "finishing" — that's not a failure, that's what this state leads to.

If you find yourself becoming fully alert again instead of drowsy, that's fine too — just let go of the exercise for tonight and rest normally.
source:
Verse: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra, verse 75.

Translation cited: Christopher Wallis ("Hareesh"), *A Translation of the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra* (2017, rev. 2018, hareesh.org).

Guided text is a modern adaptation, not a literal translation.

title: Open Horizon
essence: This is a close cousin of sky-gazing (Technique 05), but horizontal rather than vertical, and framed slightly differently in the source: less about the eyes resting on emptiness, and more about the *mind* taking on the quality of the space it's looking at — spreading out, rather than staying knotted around a single point of concern.
script:
Find a spot where you can see as far and as open a stretch as possible — the further and more featureless, the better. Standing or sitting both work.

Let your gaze settle on the open space itself, rather than on any specific object within it. If there's a building or a tree in view, let your attention pass over it rather than landing on it — you're looking *at* the openness, not *for* something in it.

Take a few breaths here. Notice the sheer amount of space in front of you compared to how much space your usual field of attention actually occupies day to day.

Let your sense of "where my attention is" widen to match what you're looking at — instead of attention feeling like a narrow beam, let it feel more like it's spread across the whole width of what you see.

If a worry or a repetitive thought shows up, notice it, then let your attention widen back out to the whole horizon rather than narrowing back down around the thought.

Stay like this for a while, letting the width of the view and the width of your attention stay loosely matched.

Before you finish, take one breath while looking at the widest part of the view, then let your gaze come back to whatever's nearby and continue your day.
source:
Verse: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra, verse 60.

Translation cited: Christopher Wallis ("Hareesh"), *A Translation of the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra* (2017, rev. 2018, hareesh.org).

Guided text is a modern adaptation, not a literal translation.

title: Steady in the Storm
essence: This is one of the few techniques in the text explicitly aimed at difficult emotional states rather than neutral or pleasant ones. It doesn't ask the practitioner to calm down before practicing — it assumes the practitioner is already activated, and offers a way to stay present inside that activation rather than either suppressing it or being swept away by it.
script:
If you're in the middle of a strong emotion right now, this is meant for exactly that moment — not for later, once you've calmed down.

Without trying to change or fix the feeling, just notice where it shows up in your body. Tight chest, hot face, clenched jaw, restless hands — wherever it is, locate it as specifically as you can.

Now, instead of pushing the feeling away or fully giving in to whatever it's telling you to do, try softening around it slightly — not the feeling itself, but the muscles around it. If your jaw is tight, soften it by ten percent, not to zero. If your shoulders are up, let them drop slightly, without forcing full relaxation.

Stay with the feeling at this slightly softer intensity for a while. You're not trying to make it disappear — you're staying present while it's here, rather than either suppressing it or acting from it immediately.

Notice whether the feeling has some shape to it — whether it rises, holds, or shifts at all, even slightly. You don't need to rush that; just notice if it starts to happen.

If the intensity eases even a little, ask yourself: what's still here, underneath the feeling, now that it's not as sharp? Often it's just a plain, quiet sense of being present — nothing dramatic, just what's left once the wave has passed through a bit.

You can return to whatever you were doing once you feel steady enough to choose your next action deliberately, rather than reacting automatically.
source:
Verse: Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra, verse 101 (the text itself cross-references verse 103 as related).

Translation cited: Christopher Wallis ("Hareesh"), *A Translation of the Vijñāna-bhairava-tantra* (2017, rev. 2018, hareesh.org).

Guided text is a modern adaptation, not a literal translation.
